titleTag: Can You Apply for a US Visa in Another Country? 2026
h1: Can You Apply for a US Visa in Another Country? What Changed in September 2025
deck: Flying somewhere with a shorter queue was the standard answer to a long wait for more than a decade. It was never banned outright, and it stopped being a good idea on 6 September 2025.
metaDescription: Third country US visa processing after the September 2025 guidance: what changed, who can still apply abroad, how to prove residence, and what happens to your fees.

Just a bad bet.
coverSpec.title: Third country US visa processing after the September 2025 guidance: still possible, no longer sensible
coverSpec.desc: On 6 September 2025, updated 10 October 2025, the State Department directed nonimmigrant visa applicants to schedule at the post in their country of nationality or legal residence. It is guidance rather than a prohibition, and existing appointments were generally not cancelled, but applicants scheduling elsewhere are warned they may find it more difficult to qualify, and fees are neither refunded nor transferred. Applicants using their country of residence must be prepared to demonstrate it.

faq.q: Is it illegal to apply for a US visa in another country?
faq.a: No, and that distinction matters. The State Department issued guidance, not a prohibition. Applicants are directed to schedule at the post in their country of nationality or legal residence, and existing third country appointments were generally not cancelled. What changed is that the department warned applicants who schedule elsewhere that they might find it more difficult to qualify for the visa. It is still possible, it is simply a much worse bet than it was.

faq.q: When did third country US visa processing change?
faq.a: On 6 September 2025, effective immediately, with an update published on 10 October 2025. Before that date, applying at a post outside your home country was a well established route, and the UAE, Canada, Mexico and Thailand were all heavily used by applicants escaping long queues at home.

faq.q: What counts as my country of residence?
faq.a: Where you actually live, on a status that allows it, rather than where you happen to be travelling. The State Department states that applicants applying in their country of residence rather than their country of nationality must be prepared to demonstrate that residence. In practice that means a residence permit or long-term visa, and the ordinary evidence of a life there: a tenancy or property, employment, bank activity, family. A tourist entry does not make you resident anywhere.

faq.q: Do I get my fee back if I apply in the wrong country?
faq.a: No. The MRV fee is non-refundable and non-transferable, and the guidance states plainly that fees paid are neither refunded nor transferred between posts. That is the financial core of this: you pay the fee, book the flights and accommodation, and if the plan does not work none of it comes back. Layering an optional expedite fee on top only increases what is at risk.

It does not apply to applicants for A, G, C-2, C-3 or NATO visas, or to diplomatic and official categories. There is also limited allowance for exceptions on humanitarian or medical emergency grounds, and for foreign policy reasons. Separately, nationals of countries where the US is not conducting routine nonimmigrant visa operations are directed to a designated post, unless their residence is somewhere else.

faq.q: I live abroad on a work permit. Which post do I use?
faq.a: The one in the country where you live. That is the whole point of the residence limb of the guidance, and for expatriates it is the reassuring half of the news: an Indian national resident in the UAE applies in the UAE, and a Filipino national resident in Canada applies in Canada. Be ready to show the residence, because you may be asked to.

faq.q: Can I still fly to Canada to use the $750 paid expedite?
faq.a: Not usefully. The expedite fee buys an earlier interview at a participating mission, currently Mission Mexico and Mission Canada, but it does not change where you are supposed to apply. An applicant resident elsewhere who books in Canada and pays $750 has spent the application fee and the expedite fee, neither of which is refundable, on an appointment the department has already advised against. It is the most expensive version of this mistake.

cta.heading: If the exit is closed, the queue at home is the whole game
cta.body: That is the practical result of the 2025 guidance for most applicants, and it is why rescheduling matters more now than it did two years ago. You cannot leave the queue, so the only lever left is working it. If you do not have the time or the hours to do that yourself, our team can take it on for your post. Tell us where you are applying, your current date and the widest range you could accept, and we will tell you honestly whether it is worth paying us at all.
